Situation1: It seems your friend is confused about the meeting spot, and you need to send a message right now to confirm it.
Expectation2: Assist patients with daily living activities such as bathing, dressing, and eating
Situation2: A patient is recovering from a recent surgery and requires more careful assistance to move and get dressed.
Story: My phone buzzes in my pocket just as I’m helping Mr. Lee, who’s still weak from surgery, sit up on the edge of his bed. He winces, and I steady him, careful not to pull too hard on his arm. Out of the corner of my eye, I see another message from Maya flash across my screen. She’s probably waiting at the wrong entrance, and I know she gets anxious when plans are unclear. I promised her I’d be there for her, especially after our last misunderstanding. But right now, Mr. Lee is looking at me, trusting me to help him get dressed without causing pain. My hands are busy, and my mind is racing. I feel the weight of Maya’s expectation for a quick reply, the need to clear things up before she gets upset again. At the same time, I can’t just leave Mr. Lee half-dressed and vulnerable. My heart pounds as I try to figure out how to be a good friend and a responsible nursing assistant at the same time, feeling pulled in two directions, knowing I can’t meet both needs at once.
